name: SPICE
description: The open-source display protocol built into QEMU/KVM hypervisors (Proxmox, oVirt, libvirt) for accessing a virtual machine's console — not a general-purpose remote desktop tool, but the native way to see and control a VM's screen, including pre-boot BIOS/bootloader access.

Wayland Unattended Access.comment: The SPICE guest agent (spice-vdagent) does not support clipboard sync or resolution sync on Wayland guests; a fix is still in progress upstream

P2P (Direct Connection).comment: The client connects directly to the SPICE server exposed by the hypervisor

Relay Server.comment: No built-in relay/NAT traversal mechanism; typically reached via the hypervisor's management network or a manual reverse proxy/tunnel

Open Source.comment: Fully open source (LGPL/GPL/BSD-style licensing), originally released by Red Hat in 2009

Multi-Monitor Support.comment: The QXL virtual display adapter supports multiple heads/monitors for a single VM

Audio Streaming.comment: Audio playback from the guest is supported

Microphone Passthrough.comment: Audio recording (client mic to guest) is supported alongside audio playback

Adaptive Bitrate.comment: Automatically adjusts image compression/quality to available bandwidth

H.264 Codec.comment: Supported for video regions via GStreamer-based streaming, in addition to still-image compression for the rest of the screen

Session Sharing.comment: Multiple simultaneous client connections are an experimental/debug feature (SPICE_DEBUG_ALLOW_MC), not enabled by default

Multi-User Sessions.comment: Native by design — each VM is its own isolated session; this isn't RDP-style multi-session on a single OS instance

Virtual Display.comment: Core to how SPICE works — the QXL virtual display adapter is the guest's video device

4:4:4 Chroma Subsampling.comment: Lossless compression modes (QUIC/GLZ/LZ4) preserve full color fidelity for UI content, unlike video-oriented 4:2:0 codecs

Frame Rate (FPS).comment: Depends on the guest's virtual GPU (QXL/virtio-gpu) and network; no fixed cap

Session Recording.comment: Not part of the protocol itself

ISO Mounting.comment: Handled by the hypervisor (e.g. Proxmox), not by the SPICE protocol itself

Wake-on-LAN.comment: Not applicable — VMs are started via the hypervisor, not woken over the network

Pre-Login Access.comment: Since SPICE renders the guest's raw framebuffer, it shows BIOS/bootloader/login screens just like a physical console

No Account Required.comment: Depends on the hypervisor's configuration — access can rely on a SPICE server password or the management layer's own authentication (e.g. Proxmox ticket)

KVM Integration.comment: Refers to hardware KVM-over-IP capture/control boards, not the KVM hypervisor SPICE is commonly paired with — these are unrelated uses of "KVM"

Shared Clipboard.comment: Works well via spice-vdagent on X11 guests; broken/unsupported on Wayland guests

SSO / OIDC.comment: Not part of the protocol; handled (if at all) by the hypervisor's management layer, e.g. Proxmox's own auth realms

2FA / MFA.comment: Not part of the protocol; would come from the hypervisor's management UI, not SPICE itself

Audit Logs.comment: Not part of the protocol; the hypervisor may log VM console access separately

Mass Deployment.comment: Not applicable at the protocol level

RBAC.comment: Not part of the protocol; access control is managed by the hypervisor (e.g. Proxmox permissions)

Remote Printing.comment: No native print-redirection driver; a physical USB printer could in theory be passed through via USB redirection

Generic USB Passthrough.comment: USB redirection (usbredir) is one of SPICE's marquee features, working at a low protocol level for arbitrary USB devices

File Manager UI.comment: No dedicated two-pane file manager, though spice-vdagent supports drag-and-drop file transfer into the guest

Proxy Support.comment: No native proxy setting; the connection can be manually tunneled (e.g. over SSH) but this isn't a built-in protocol feature

UAC Handling.comment: Since SPICE streams the guest's raw framebuffer, UAC prompts on a Windows guest display normally without any special handling

OTA Updates.comment: Not applicable — SPICE is a protocol/library, updated via the host OS's package manager, not an OTA mechanism

Windows: Host.comment: SPICE has no notion of a physical-desktop "host" — the server side is a library used by Linux-based hypervisors (QEMU/KVM), not something you run to share a Windows desktop

Windows: Client.comment: virt-viewer/remote-viewer builds are available for Windows

macOS: Host.comment: Same reasoning as Windows: Host — not applicable

macOS: Client.comment: virt-viewer builds exist for macOS but are less commonly maintained/used than the Linux and Windows clients

Linux X11: Host.comment: This is the "native" case — the SPICE server runs as part of QEMU/KVM on a Linux hypervisor host

Linux Wayland: Host.comment: The hypervisor host itself runs fine under Wayland; the limitation is specifically with Wayland inside the guest VM (clipboard/resolution sync)

Linux: Client.comment: virt-viewer/remote-viewer are native on Linux and the most common way to use SPICE

Android: Client.comment: Third-party SPICE clients exist for Android (e.g. aSPICE), not an official first-party app

iOS: Client.comment: Limited third-party SPICE client support exists on iOS

Web Browser: Client.comment: spice-html5 is an experimental JavaScript/WebSocket client; Proxmox's own web console typically uses noVNC rather than full SPICE-over-browser

NVIDIA RTX 4090.comment: SPICE performance depends on the guest's virtual GPU (QXL/virtio-gpu), not host GPU passthrough benchmarks, in typical deployments

Free Tier.comment: Completely free and open source, no tiers or paid unlocks

Enterprise.comment: SPICE itself has no paid tier; Red Hat sells support subscriptions for the virtualization platforms (e.g. RHV) it's bundled into, not for SPICE itself
